prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne’er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman’s hallo’, Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins’ russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor’s sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more agèd, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney’s box, Must soon partake his grave.

Keywords: Here, Nor, Whose

outputs.L1:
Here lies one whom no hound ever pursued,  
Nor fleetest greyhound followed;  
Whose foot never stained the morning dew,  
Nor ear heard the huntsman’s hallo:  

Old Tiney, surliest of his kind,  
Who, though nursed with tender care  
And confined within domestic bounds,  
Remained a wild jack-hare.  

Though nightly from my hand he took  
His modest portion of food,  
He did so with a wary, jealous look,  
And, whenever he could, would bite.  

His fare was wheaten bread,  
With milk, and oats, and straw;  
Thistles, or lettuces instead,  
And sand to scour his maw.  

On hawthorn twigs he feasted,  
On the russet peel of pippins;  
And when his juicy salads failed,  
Sliced carrot pleased him well.  

A Turkey carpet was his lawn,  
Whereon he loved to bound,  
To skip and gambol like a fawn,  
And swing his rump around.  

His frisking came at evening hours,  
For then he lost his fear;  
But most before approaching showers,  
Or when a storm drew near.  

Eight years and five full-rolling moons  
He thus beheld steal away,  
Dozing through all his idle noons,  
And every night at play.  

I kept him for his humor’s sake,  
For he would often beguile  
My heart of thoughts that made it ache,  
And compel me to a smile.  

But now, beneath this walnut shade,  
He finds his long, last home,  
And waits, in snug concealment laid,  
Till gentler Puss shall come.  

He, still more aged, feels the shocks  
From which no care can save;  
And, once the partner of Tiney’s box,  
Must soon partake his grave.
outputs.L2:
Buried here is one whom no hunting dog ever chased,  
nor did any faster greyhound run after him.  
His feet never spoiled the fresh dew of morning,  
and his ears never heard a hunter’s cry.

This is old Tiney, the most ill-tempered of his breed.  
Though he was raised with gentle attention  
and kept within the limits of a tame household life,  
he remained, in spirit, a wild jack-hare.

Each night he regularly accepted from my hand  
the small portion of food allotted to him,  
yet he took it with suspicion in his eyes,  
and, whenever he had the chance, he would bite.

He ate wheaten bread, milk, oats, and straw;  
sometimes thistles or lettuces served instead,  
and sand was provided to cleanse his stomach.

He enjoyed nibbling hawthorn twigs  
and the russet skins of pippin apples.  
When his fresh green meals were lacking,  
thin slices of carrot satisfied him well enough.

A Turkey carpet served as his meadow,  
and there he delighted in leaping about,  
skipping and playing like a young deer,  
while swinging his hindquarters as he moved.

He usually became lively in the evening,  
for at that hour his fear lessened.  
He was especially playful before rainstorms,  
or whenever rough weather was coming near.

In this manner he passed eight years  
and five full months,  
sleeping through his quiet, idle afternoons  
and spending every night in play.

I kept him because of his odd character,  
for he often distracted my mind  
from painful thoughts  
and compelled me to smile.

But now, under the shade of this walnut tree,  
he has found his final resting place,  
lying hidden away in comfort  
until gentler Puss shall join him.

Puss, even older than Tiney, now feels the blows  
that no care can ultimately prevent;  
once the companion of Tiney’s box,  
he too must soon share his grave.
outputs.L3:
Old Tiney was a domesticated jack-hare, though he never truly became tame. However carefully he was treated, and however tenderly he was cared for, he kept much of his wild nature. He remained surly, cautious, and distrustful, as if he could never quite believe that the hands feeding him meant no harm.

Each evening, Tiney would accept food from his keeper, but even this he did with suspicion. He came near only in his own guarded way, watching closely and ready to defend himself. If an unwary hand came too close, he would bite whenever he had the chance, proving that affection and captivity had not softened his stubborn spirit.

His meals were varied and generous. He was fed bread and milk, oats and straw, and he enjoyed rougher fare such as thistles and hawthorn twigs. Lettuce, apple peel, and carrots were also part of his diet, offering him a mixture of household scraps, garden produce, and the kinds of plants a hare might have found for himself in the wild.

Though he slept away much of the day, Tiney came alive in the evenings. Then he would play and gambol about indoors, moving with sudden bursts of energy and liveliness. He was especially active before storms, as if the changing weather stirred some instinct within him. At such times, his wildness seemed less like bad temper and more like a reminder of the free creature he had once been.

Despite his difficult nature, the speaker cherished Tiney deeply. His presence brought comfort, amusement, and many smiles. Now that he is gone, those memories are touched with sadness. Old Tiney lies buried beneath a walnut tree, mourned not because he was gentle or obedient, but because he was himself: untamed, spirited, and dearly loved.
outputs.L4:
The poem serves as a memorial to Old Tiney, a tame jack-hare who lived close to human beings but never entirely lost his wild and independent nature. Rather than presenting him as a simple pet, the speaker remembers him in detail, carefully describing his character, his habits, and the small routines that made him distinctive. Tiney is shown as difficult, stubborn, and sometimes ill-tempered, yet also full of life. His behavior is unpredictable: he accepts care and shelter, but he remains spirited and resistant to complete domestication.

The speaker recalls Tiney’s diet and daily habits as part of this affectionate portrait. These ordinary details make the hare seem vivid and real, not merely symbolic. His eating, resting, and movements around the household reveal a creature with a strong personality of his own. In the evenings, especially, Tiney becomes playful and animated, bringing energy and amusement into the speaker’s life. His liveliness offers companionship and comfort, even though he is not always gentle or easy to manage.

Because of this, Tiney’s death carries emotional weight. He dies beneath the shade of a walnut tree, a peaceful image that nevertheless emphasizes the sadness of his passing. The speaker’s grief suggests that Tiney’s presence had become an important part of daily life. His loss is not only the death of an animal but the disappearance of a familiar companion whose difficult, lively nature had helped relieve loneliness and melancholy.

The poem also widens its meaning by mentioning Puss, Tiney’s surviving companion. Tiney’s death becomes a reminder that all living creatures are subject to mortality, even those whose daily habits once seemed permanent and reassuring. For the speaker, and perhaps for Puss as well, the hare’s passing marks the fragility of companionship and the inevitable loss that follows attachment. In this way, the poem transforms a personal memory of a beloved animal into a quiet reflection on affection, grief, and death.
